evidence.fact: Forestry advisory tools that combine remote sensing with AI already exist. Södra and Terra Labs' AI planner builds forest management plans, and Finnish chatbot-style advisors combine forest data, costs and legal requirements into recommendations. These tools speed up advisory work but are not meant to replace foresters.
In Alabama, anyone who gives forest management recommendations for hire on land they do not own must be registered with the state Board of Registration for Foresters.
California's Board of Forestry says that offering forestry recommendations on forested land without a Registered Professional Forester's expertise and stamp violates the Professional Foresters Law.

Jail management systems already automate parts of the release check. Tyler's DeKalb deployment halved release processing time and removed duplicate warrant data entry, and other systems recheck charges and warrants (NCIC) at release. Because warrant databases are split across agencies, a human still has to cross-check.
Deschutes County jail policy names the shift supervisor as the final safeguard in the release process. The supervisor must sign the Release Authorization Form before an inmate is released.
In Bexar County, two supervisors must approve each release, and staff who authorize a wrongful release can be disciplined. Legal accountability therefore stays with human supervisors.
The main salon platforms (Fresha, Boulevard, Vagaro, Mindbody) can keep a client's card on file and take deposits automatically. That lets software settle a bill without anyone at the counter.
Boulevard offers a self-checkout kiosk and an AI receptionist. Third-party AI receptionists connect to Vagaro's API to find clients, book appointments and take deposits.

The vendor sources say AI tools handle booking and deposits, but they don't confirm fully automatic checkout after a visit. Taking cash, making change and helping clients with tap or chip payments at the till still need a person there.

Shelf-scanning robots such as Simbe's Tally and Walmart's scanners find out-of-stock items, wrong prices and label problems on shelves. They give information to store associates, but people still do the physical cleaning and organizing. These are robots, which the reference AI agent does not have.
In 2026, agentic AI in retail is used for customer support, pricing and clienteling. It is described as a tool that helps associates, not as something that sells on the sales floor.
Walmart says its in-store inventory robots check shelves but will not replace store workers. The physical shelf work and selling face to face still need people.

Salesforce made its Agentforce Commerce Shopper Agent generally available in mid-2026 (June 24 or July 6; the sources give different dates). The agent answers consumer product questions, helps them find products and handles checkout on the retailer's own storefront.

The agents connect directly to inventory, order and customer data, so they can explain products and deal with service questions without passing the customer to a person. Commentators warn that answers drawn from the product catalogue can still be wrong, and no independent accuracy data was found.

Salesforce says AI influenced 20% of global online sales ($262B) during the 2025 holiday season. These are vendor figures. In physical stores, showing how a product works and building trust face to face still needs a person on the floor.

Industry commentary from 2026 says agentic AI can take a learning objective to a finished course: it analyzes source material, structures the content, builds personalized learning paths, role-plays and rubrics, and loads the course into an LMS. This evidence is mostly vendor or industry commentary, not independent outcome studies.

Courses on AI-powered instructional design for L&D professionals stress that human expertise is still essential for learning strategy and quality. These are marketing listings, not evidence of outcomes.

Canada's Job Bank lists Manager, Training and Development as not regulated. US career guides describe certification such as ATD or ISPI as voluntary, so no licence is generally required. A few roles, such as security training, have employer-specific credential requirements.

Coats Digital released GSD RealMotion in August 2026. It is an AI tool that turns shop-floor video into method studies and is designed to work alongside its existing GSDCost system. The vendor (not independent testing) says it cuts a 45-minute manual timing exercise to about 15 minutes. So AI speeds up key steps, but someone still has to film on the floor and check the results.

A proposed framework for AI-assisted MODAPTS calls for checking AI-generated standards against stopwatch or video time studies, with manual recoding when they differ by more than ±5%. That means a human still has to validate the work before standards are used.

In the US, industrial engineers usually don't need a PE license because many states have an industrial exemption. A license is generally needed only for stamping designs. So in most cases, no law or license requires a human to sign off on internal labor standards or cost systems.

Existing AI tools such as aiScout (ai.io), Hudl, Sportlogiq and Wyscout already analyze athlete video, score drills and generate performance data and scouting reports. This covers the record-review and much of the skill-assessment work.

A 2024 study of English academy scouts found no significant difference between ratings made in person and from video. However, scouts still considered in-person viewing more accurate, and it carries real time and travel costs.

Scouts still value live viewing for intangibles (work ethic, leadership, body language, off-ball behaviour) and use in-person events and tryouts. Evaluating physical fitness on site requires being there. No search result showed a licensing rule requiring a human scout.

Raman systems like PharmID Verify check what is inside IV bags, syringes and vials, but the vendor describes them as helping pharmacists with final checks. The work still needs someone physically handling the product, and the verification is the pharmacist's.

A pilot study in 2016 found Raman testing of compounded preparations had a 100% positive predictive value. These are instrument tests run on physical samples, not tasks an agent can do with software alone.

Under USP <795> and state rules (for example N.J.A.C. 13:39-11A.10), the licensed compounding pharmacist is responsible for the identity, strength, quality and purity of ingredients and preparations, including inspecting them and reviewing the Certificate of Analysis.
JailTracker's jail management software sends automated alerts about inmate appointments and transfers, and its scheduler module keeps staff up to date on scheduled inmate activities and appointments.
InCustody schedules inmate visitation appointments, keeps visitor history and enforces visitation rules, so the rule-based booking step is already software-driven.

A Virginia regional jail moved visitation scheduling from handwritten weekly logs to online self-booking, which shows the scheduling work itself is digital and needs no physical presence. Officers still oversee security limits such as keep-away orders, lockdowns and movement.

Corrections scheduling tools such as VCS COSS, UKG TeleStaff and InTime automate shift rotations, post assignments, overtime and compliance with minimum staffing, but they are rules-based and assist the supervisor rather than replace them.

Housing sergeants act as first-line supervisors on the unit. They brief staff at the start of each shift, make sure officers follow post orders, conduct inmate counts and step in on disciplinary problems, all of which require being physically present in the facility.

Corrections sergeants are sworn positions in a defined chain of command. They supervise, direct, discipline and evaluate officers, which puts personnel and security accountability on a human supervisor.

Restaurant inventory software sold by vendors (Crunchtime/Fourth iQ 2.2) is said to forecast when key items will run out and send '86' alerts for missing ingredients. An agent could do this reconciliation, forecasting and shortage reporting from POS and inventory data.
Bar loss-detection software such as BarGuard is described as comparing poured amounts against sold amounts, flagging likely over-pours or missing items, and sending reorder notices automatically.

Counting stock still means a person walks the cooler, freezer, dry storage and bar, counts or weighs bottles and checks kegs. An agent with no body cannot do this step, so a human must stay involved. Source is vendor content.

Kitchen automation in 2026 runs on dedicated robot hardware such as Appetronix arms for portioning, plating and salad or bowl assembly. Software-only agents can't do it, and the search found no system aimed at making hors d'oeuvres.
Automated micro kitchens cover only fixed modules (frying, baking, salads, stir-fry), and they are physical robotic systems, not AI agents.

Cooking robots like SoftBank's STEAMA and FLAMA need physical hardware on site. That confirms the task means handling food in person; a software agent can only help with recipes, scaling and prep lists.

In nursing-home rules, the interdisciplinary team that reviews and revises the care plan must include the nurse aide responsible for the resident. The aide's role is to report firsthand observations from contact with the resident, not to write the plan.

Vendor AI tools (StoriiCare) draft care plans from assessments and progress notes, and staff review the drafts before finalizing them. This shows AI can help with the documentation and summary parts of a review.
Home-care platforms predict AI agents will handle documentation, risk detection and information routing for care teams in 2026. Clinical judgement and the team discussion stay with people.

According to vendor descriptions, AI agents extract unit price, tooling, MOQ, lead time and freight terms from quotes in any format and convert them to a common delivered cost basis. These are product claims, not independent evaluations.
One vendor guide describes an agent that checks current supplier pricing for a materials list and applies the firm's markup, overhead allocation and profit rules.
Quote-extraction tools such as Procumi have the user review and confirm extracted data before it is saved. Scanned PDFs and inconsistent item descriptions are known weak points.

Teller-platform software such as CheckPartner Enterprise and TROY AssurePay Teller takes the teller's request, sends the official check to a secure MICR printer and emails larger amounts to a manager for approval. That digitizes the data entry, funds and debit posting, and approval steps, but someone still has to handle the check stock, sign or endorse the check, and give it to the customer.

Cloud official-check software integrates with the core banking system and uses multi-factor authentication. An agent would only have access to these issuance and verification systems if the bank granted it credentials.

Remote official-check issuance with secure printing is already offered, so preparation can be centralized. Under bank internal-control policies, an authorized human signer or approver is still accountable for official checks, especially high-value ones.

Vendor material says AI cash-application agents can take payment details from lockbox PDFs, bank files and remittance emails, match them, and post payments to the ERP with little manual data entry. This covers the recording step. These are vendor claims and have not been checked independently.
HighRadius describes specialized agents that download bank statements and lockbox files and post payments to the ERP. That means software already does the recording and reconciliation sub-steps.

Paper checks and money orders still have to be physically received and scanned by staff, or sent to a mail-in or lockbox service, before they can be deposited. So the 'send items for processing' step needs a person or physical equipment.

AI scheduling engines use real-time location, skill match, traffic and parts availability to build and rebuild schedules automatically. One guide cites Geotab's 2025 report saying 76% of field-service leaders already use AI scheduling and dispatch.
Agentic AI dispatch connects to telematics and IoT sensors to monitor locations and coordinate assignments. Vendors say fully autonomous loops are only in pilots, and they name no customers.

Adaptive scheduling keeps recalculating assignments as technician availability, job priority and traffic change. This is a software-only task that needs no physical presence and no licensed human sign-off.

Vendor material says procurement agents can draft purchase orders from approved requests and check them against budget and contract terms, but a human buyer still releases each order. Other vendors describe spending caps and limits as guardrails. These are vendor claims.
A practitioner source says agentic AI in procurement is mostly used in pilots and narrow cases. Unusual price variances are typically handed off to a human.

A CMMS vendor says AI analytics can forecast maintenance costs 12 to 24 months ahead from historical spend, PM schedules and asset age. This supports automated spend monitoring and budget input, but the claim comes from the vendor.

O*NET lists this as a core task for Helpers--Installation, Maintenance, and Repair Workers (49-9098.00). It is hands-on work: cleaning and lubricating vehicles, machinery, tools and work areas with hand tools, power tools and cleaning equipment.

The other core tasks in this occupation are physical too, such as installing or replacing parts with hand or power tools, moving tools and supplies between work stations, and applying protective coatings against corrosion. This leaves almost nothing a software-only agent with no body could do. At most it could look up lubrication schedules or specs, which is a small share of the time.
No licence or sign-off rule requires a human for routine cleaning and lubrication. The barrier is entirely physical.
Valet job descriptions list greeting arriving guests and opening the passenger doors as core duties. Both are done in person, by hand, at the curb.
A state job description has attendants greet guests, open vehicle doors, explain valet procedures and tag keys at the vehicle. These steps happen face to face.
Valet setups without attendants use kiosks and robots to handle check-in and parking. They do away with the human greeting and door service. No software-only AI agent opens car doors.

Commercial SPC software, including Minitab Real-Time SPC, already monitors production data and flags process variation. AI tools (from vendors whose claims are unverified) say they can turn raw files and logs into control charts on their own.
No US license is specifically required for quality control technicians. Certification such as ASQ CQT is voluntary, so no legal sign-off barrier applies to the statistical analysis itself.
QA sign-off and review of production documentation are duties set by the employer. In practice, a human still checks the data's provenance and the reliability conclusions before acting on them.

Client-facing benefit chatbots already exist, such as Connecticut DSS's 'Laurel'. It answers common questions, checks benefit status, pre-screens eligibility and gives guided help with applications. Code for America and Anthropic are also building a Claude-based SNAP Policy Navigator that answers caseworkers' policy questions.

On a public-benefits SNAP benchmark (September 2026), the best model scored about 77%, so roughly a quarter of its answers were still wrong. Its advice needs to be grounded in state-specific policy and checked by a human.

Job specs for this role list home visits, hands-on teaching of budgeting, meal prep and housecleaning, and escorting clients. The work is done under a supervising professional, but the assistant does not need a licence.

NPS Conserve O Gram 17/3 describes cavity-packing objects in boxes that float inside a shipping crate, and marking foam with directions for removal and placement. This is hands-on work with the object and the packing materials.

Gallery Systems' TMS Collections has a Shipping module that groups objects into crates and produces shipping reports, crate lists and valuation documents. The paperwork side of the task can be done in software, but the physical packing cannot.

An NPS/Harpers Ferry registrar guide says that before packing, staff should assess each object's surface and structure and note weak points and earlier repairs. That is a physical inspection, though building the master list of catalog numbers, sizes and weights is clerical work an agent could support.

XTEN-AV's own product pages say its AI-assisted X-DRAW tool generates signal-flow diagrams, rack layouts, speaker layouts, bills of materials and cable schedules. This is the vendor's claim and was not independently verified, but it suggests an agent can draft the layout-design part of the task.

O*NET lists this task as a core duty of Audio and Video Technicians, next to setting up, maintaining and taking down physical equipment such as microphones, speakers, cables, mixing boards and cameras.

Employer job descriptions require hands-on work, such as using 16 ft ladders to reach projectors, speakers and wiring in ceilings. This makes the upgrade and maintenance part physical work that an agent cannot do.

AOTA guidance and state OT rules say an OTA may administer standardized assessments only after service competency is established, under a supervising OT who directs the evaluation and interprets the results. A licensed human therefore stays accountable for the testing.

Tablet-based tests and AI or computer-vision scoring of cognitive and motor skills exist but are still being validated against standard tests given by human examiners (for example TGMD-3, NEPSY-II and ATEC). Agents can help with scoring, recording and drafting reports, but not with the hands-on situational testing.

The OT supervision guidelines describe OTA services as delivered in person and in a supervised partnership. Situational testing means setting up materials, physically guarding and cueing the client, and observing the client directly.
O*NET lists 'Arrange treatment supplies to keep them in order' as a physical therapist aide task, done next to hands-on work like cleaning the work area and disinfecting equipment after treatment.
Aides keep linen and supplies stocked and tell a manager when more stock needs ordering. Supplies are physically handled in the clinic under PT/PTA supervision.
Clinic inventory software (low-stock alerts, vendor and order tracking) can handle only the digital tracking and reordering side. It cannot physically arrange supplies.

RFID uniform and linen systems such as InvoTech GIMS track items as they move, count laundry carts and storerooms with fixed and handheld readers, and keep a running uniform count in a central database. This automates record-keeping but still needs staff to tag, scan and handle items.
A vendor case study from Ocean Resort Casino reports about 50% lower labor costs from automating uniform and linen inventory. Physical handling and issuing of items still happens on site.

LinenTech advertises RFID inventory counts with automatic reordering, the digital part an agent could take over (reconciling records, reordering). Counting, sorting and storing the items themselves needs a person on site.

Mortuary cosmetic work means hands-on restorative art on the body, such as styling hair, applying makeup, covering bruises and rebuilding features. Several sources say a cosmetologist, funeral director or embalmer license is required, but these are career guides, not official licensing boards.

Funeral-industry AI tools found, such as the Tukios AI Photo Engine (launched February 2026), only edit tribute photos digitally. No software or agent was found that applies cosmetics to the deceased.
Embalmer licensing usually requires a mortuary science program, the NBFSE board exam and often an apprenticeship. An older (2005) California code lists restorative art among the exam subjects.

Off-the-shelf tour operator software such as TourOperation already takes payments in several currencies, issues QR-coded tickets, sends WhatsApp and SMS notices and produces reconciliation reports. An agent could run these steps: payment links, reminders, tracking who has paid and reconciliation.

Viagilize offers online payment by PIX and credit card, QR check-in for boarding and attendance, and a portal for guides. This automates collecting fees ahead of time, but someone still has to scan or check tickets on site.
UltimaTour Operator supports offline payments, mobile check-in and taking attendance in person. Collecting cash and paper tickets from group members on site still needs a person there.

Vendors describe AI voice agents that place outbound calls, hold full conversations, handle basic objections, book meetings and log results to the CRM without a human. Follow-up of leads who have already shown interest is described as the strongest use; these figures come from vendors.

Vendor benchmarks say 28-34% of mid-market and enterprise B2B sales teams used AI voice agents for outbound calling as of Q1 2026. They also report that AI voice follow-up got prospects to act more often than email.

In a February 2024 ruling, the FCC said AI-generated voices count as 'artificial or prerecorded voice' under the TCPA. Marketing calls using them need prior express written consent, which closes the 'live human' exception for AI callers. Calls without that consent effectively have to be made by a human.

Commercial systems already send automated text-to-voice alerts from video analytics and access-control alarms to security staff's two-way radios, and staff can acknowledge them from the radio. This means the contact step can be done in software without a human keying the radio.

BearCom AlwaysOn turns standard two-way radio systems into an interface between people and machines. Machines and software can talk on the same radio network as human operators, so an agent could reach security staff if it is connected to such a gateway.

A patented speech-based two-way radio assistant uses a computer to control a radio base station, hear speech on the channel and speak replies back. This shows two-way voice exchanges over radio can be automated. Without such a radio-over-IP or push-to-talk-over-cellular gateway, though, an ordinary handheld or desk radio is out of an agent's reach.

Banks already let customers order foreign cash themselves online, with shipping or branch pickup. That automates the order, rate quote and payment steps. A clerk is still needed to physically hand over cash at the counter.

US Bank Secrecy Act rules require the bank to verify the customer's identity and keep a log for sales of monetary instruments such as traveler's checks paid in cash between $3,000 and $10,000. Cash transactions over $10,000 need a Currency Transaction Report. Checking the ID document usually happens in person at the counter.

Rules for foreign exchange and traveler's cheque transactions require identity checks above set thresholds. That means looking at physical ID documents, while the cash itself must be counted, checked and handed over.

O*NET lists this as a core task for Helpers–Electricians (importance 77). The related tasks are all hands-on: stripping and terminating wire, cutting and bending conduit, carrying materials to the job site, taking apart defective equipment and cleaning the work area. A software-only agent cannot do any of these. At most it can look up procedures or specs, which is a very small share of the work.

In Maine, licensed helper electricians may do installations only under the direct supervision of a master, journeyman or limited electrician who employs them. So a licensed human carries responsibility for the work.

Hawaii lets helpers and other unlicensed people do electrical work only under a licensed journey worker or supervising electrician, who must be physically present at the project site the whole time the work is done.

O*NET lists Helpers--Electricians (47-3013.00) as hands-on support work: stripping insulation, attaching wires to terminals and helping electricians on site. Soldering with an iron means physically handling wires, solder and a heated tool.

The task 'Solder electrical connections, using soldering iron' shows up on job-board copies of the O*NET helpers-electricians profile. It is a physical step on the job, and a software-only agent has no way to do it.

O*NET lists 'Clean shop, work area, and machines, using solvent and rags' as a core task for Helpers--Pipelayers, Plumbers, Pipefitters, and Steamfitters. It is a hands-on cleaning duty done in the shop or on the job site.

O*NET says workers in this occupation help plumbers, pipefitters, steamfitters and pipelayers by doing less-skilled manual work, such as supplying or holding materials and tools and cleaning the work area and equipment. All of this requires being there in person.
O*NET lists this as a task for furnace, kiln and oven operators: cleaning and oiling equipment with scrapers, solvents and air hoses. It is hands-on maintenance work done in person.
Related tasks for this job include clearing jams with hand tools, replacing worn parts and removing ash with shovels and buckets. These all need someone physically at the equipment.
Furnace-wall cleaning equipment is a hand-operated pneumatic tool run by one person, not a software system. An AI agent without robotics could at most look up maintenance schedules or manuals.

Restaurant inventory software such as Restaurant365 can set par levels, send low-stock alerts and build suggested purchase orders. This covers only the digital tracking around restocking. The actual wiping, sanitizing and carrying stock to the line still needs a person's hands.

Food-code-based state rules require food-contact surfaces to be cleaned and sanitized at set intervals, about every 4 hours for TCS food, and whenever contamination may have occurred. These rules set when the work happens but do not require a licensed person to do it.
Digital cleaning-schedule and checklist tools exist for food safety operations. They schedule and log the cleaning but do not perform it.

Zoo Atlanta used an AI Animal Assistant from Satisfi Labs. It answered visitors' questions about species, where exhibits are, and daily feeding schedules and activities, using facts from the zoo's own database.

At Madrid Zoo, a virtual keeper called IrenIA appears on a screen beside the panda enclosure. It answers visitors' questions about the animals and the facility in Spanish and English. That puts on-site question answering in AI hands, but the question is still answered at the exhibit.

A Mysuru Zoo assistant answers in five languages and bases its replies on the zoo's own information about animals, timings, facilities and rules. The vendor reports a large rise in handled queries, but nobody outside the vendor has checked that figure.

Calf milk calculators and ration-formulation software already do the calculation part of the task: amounts, concentrations and adjusting feeding for calf weight, age and ingredient supply. A human still has to measure and mix the food or formula.

Veterinary compounding rules tie drug preparation and use to a veterinarian's prescription and supervision. The caretaker follows existing instructions and does not sign for them, so the main barrier is physical work, not licensing.

Kentucky allows a veterinarian or a licensed veterinary technician to administer compounded veterinary drugs. In this task, medication is prepared from a veterinarian's prescription rather than prescribed by the caretaker.

Since 2022 the IRS has used AI voice bots for collection calls. Taxpayers who received notices can confirm their identity with a PIN and set up or change payment plans, and the bots also explain notices and answer common questions.
The IRS reported that its voice bots handled over 4.8 million calls, with about 40% resolved without a human. Callers who wanted a person could still ask to reach a live assistor.

Calls from mailed collection notices went to the ACS voice bot, which set up payment plans for balances under $25,000. Early on, the share of calls resolved without a human was about 30%, below the 40% target.

As of 2026, agentic tools can find funding opportunities, draft proposals and check them against funder rules (for example GRAIL and the SciSpace NSF agent). Guidance and testing still recommend that people write the core scientific narrative, because reviewers notice generic AI prose.

NIH notice NOT-OD-25-132 says NIH will not treat applications substantially developed by AI as the applicant's original ideas. This is reported by a secondary comparison site and was not checked against the notice itself.

NSF asks proposers to disclose generative-AI use and holds authors responsible for the accuracy of AI-assisted content. An Authorized Organizational Representative must certify the proposal when it is submitted.

Scite, Elicit, Consensus and Scopus AI pull real citations from scholarly databases (Semantic Scholar, Scopus) and summarize them, so the search-and-compile sub-steps of a bibliography can already be automated.

These tools do not show journal quality metrics, and coverage varies (Scopus AI defaults to post-2013 studies). A human still has to check source credibility and whether each item suits the course, so the output needs instructor review before use.

Library guides present AI tools as aids for literature discovery that need human checking. Neither guide mentions any legal or licensing rule that a human must compile or sign a reading list. The task is fully digital, though some full texts sit behind subscriptions.

Vendor pages (not checked against Instructure's own documentation) say AI agents can write scores into the Canvas gradebook through LTI Assignment and Grade Services, within the permission scopes set up for them, while Canvas remains the official record for grades. Integration platforms describe automatic enrollment sync and scheduled gradebook-to-SIS pushes. My search found nothing on automating attendance or roll call.

The instructor of record is responsible for making sure final grades are submitted for every enrolled student by the deadline. FERPA limits posting grades by name or identifiable number. This responsibility comes from university policy, not from a FERPA clause.
At WSU, submitting grades requires a current FERPA certification and the department listing you as instructor of record, so access is tied to a named, credentialed person.

Gemini in Google Classroom can draft rubrics from the assignment context and suggest personalized feedback on written work. Teachers review and edit this output before using it. AI agents can therefore create assignments, score objective and written work, and draft feedback, but the AI's work is still checked by the teacher.

District policy in Dorchester District Two (South Carolina) says AI cannot be the sole basis for a grade. Teachers must review the work and make the final call, so a human keeps the essential sign-off step.

Illinois Senate Bill 416 would bar teachers from using AI to grade student work. This shows legal and accountability pressure to keep grading with the teacher of record. Note: the bill's final status was not confirmed.

Vendor AI tools available in 2026 cover the side work around parent conferences: drafting talking points from student data, adjusting the tone of messages, writing emails on sensitive topics, booking conference slots and collecting parent intake information. The search found no source showing an AI running the conferences or settling behavioral or academic problems itself. The time savings come from the vendors and were not measured independently.

Scheduling and intake agents for parent-teacher conferences exist, so logistics can be handed off. The conference conversation and the decisions still involve the teacher, parents, counselors and administrators.

District guidance says FERPA covers student records, including those held by AI vendors. A vendor may receive the data only if it qualifies as a 'school official' and the school keeps direct control over it. Teachers are told to keep identifiable data such as grades and IEP or 504 information out of unapproved AI tools. This limits what an agent can work with but does not require a human to sign off on the conference.

In 2026, AI grading tools generate quizzes and grade multiple-choice, essay and STEM work against teacher rubrics, and they connect to the school's learning management system (the online course system). Examples include CoGrader, which pulls work from Google Classroom, Canvas and Schoology. That covers the test-writing step and the grading of written work.

Some vendor designs, such as OpenEduCat, keep a human in the loop: the AI suggests scores and feedback, and the teacher approves each grade before it counts. That points to partial delegation rather than full delegation.

Career and technical education is often assessed through hands-on performance tests. Students complete real jobs with the tools, materials and equipment of the trade while a skilled evaluator watches in person. An agent with no physical body cannot run or score this part.

Mediation between roommates is run in person by trained Resident Assistants. Each roommate states the issues, they discuss each other's side and propose compromises. Sessions usually take under an hour and sometimes need a second meeting.

RAs hold in-person conversations with roommates to draft and document roommate agreements. Unresolved conflicts go to Resident Directors. This means the agent's digital share is mainly drafting agreements and documentation.

Roompact and similar software only support the process. They send check-ins, flag conflicts early and alert residence life staff, and they do not replace a human mediator. No purpose-built AI mediator was found in use at residence life offices.

Jackpot handpays have traditionally needed an attendant to walk to the machine. Vendors such as JCM Global and CasinoSoft are building systems that pay jackpots by TITO ticket and handle the W-2G at the machine. That is fixed casino-floor equipment, not something a general AI agent does.

An IRS document describes the handpay steps: a casino employee verifies the jackpot at the machine and collects the winner's details for the W-2G. The IRS requires winners to show two forms of ID, one with a photo.
State regulators such as Pennsylvania's gaming board set internal controls that require employees to verify and sign off on jackpot payouts in certain dollar ranges.

The free Rangeland Analysis Platform estimates vegetation cover and herbaceous biomass from satellite imagery going back to 1986, refreshed every 16 days. Its Production Explorer shows how forage changes affect AUMs, grazing days and carrying capacity, which is analysis an agent can run from a browser.

The satellite models are calibrated against plots collected by hand. Stocking-rate tools such as StockSmart also need site inputs like distance to water, slope and how animals use the land, so someone still has to check grazing patterns in the field.

BLM rangeland management specialist postings ask for education and experience, such as monitoring livestock grazing. The excerpts reviewed did not require SRM certification or a licensed signature, though SRM offers voluntary certifications that NRCS recognizes.

AI tools for horses only analyse gait from phone video or sensors (Sleip, TrojanTrack, Horscan, HorseCare DR). The trainer still handles, rides and conditions the horse, and Sleip's output is not diagnostic: vets interpret it.
Kentucky does not let a horse race unless its trainer holds a current commission licence. To get one, the trainer must show experience and pass a standard exam given by the stewards.

Minnesota requires racing trainers to have 2 years of horsemanship experience and to pass a written exam and a practical horsemanship test. The practical test shows that the core of the work is hands-on handling of live animals.

Dallmeier's AI camera system recognizes cards and chips at baccarat and blackjack tables, and the vendor reports more than 1,000 tables in Macau. That figure comes from the vendor and was not independently checked. This shows that machines can do the hand-reading and comparison step when the table is fitted with these cameras.

Patented card-reading shoes and monitoring systems read card ranks and apply the game rules (for example in baccarat) to decide which hand wins. The judgment itself is easy to automate, but only on tables with this special hardware, which an AI agent would not normally be able to reach.

Dealers at live tables must hold a gaming license from their state. Examples include the Nevada Gaming Control Board, the Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board and the Indiana Gaming Commission. Dealers also work in person, revealing cards and settling hands at the table.

Consumer AI apps already handle intake: HairHunt uses a short quiz to build a personalised shortlist of styles, and other apps offer an AI stylist chat and photo try-ons that clients can share with their barber. An agent could run the service-and-style questioning before the visit.

Barber-facing tools such as StyleForge offer 3D hair and beard try-ons to show customers in the shop. They support the consultation, but the barber still runs it at the chair and checks hair texture, growth patterns and head shape in person.
State law requires a licence to practise barbering, meaning the physical services. Nothing found shows that law requires a licensed human to do the consultation or questioning itself.

Consumer and salon tools already analyse photos of a person's scalp and hair, identify conditions such as dryness, oiliness or hair loss, and recommend matching products or in-salon treatments. Examples are HairCoSys, L'Oréal Professionnel My Scalp ID and iHairium. These are vendor claims; I found no independent accuracy testing.

A start-up's app uses photos of the head to identify hair and scalp conditions and suggest ways to treat them. This covers the analysis-and-recommendation step from start to finish, but someone still has to take good images. In a barbershop, the barber normally checks the client's hair and scalp in person by looking and touching.

Barber licences include scalp treatments, but barbers may not practise medicine. California's board rules require licensees to stay within the areas they are licensed for, and I found no rule saying a licensed human must sign off on cosmetic product suggestions. Medical scalp conditions have to be referred to a doctor, whoever is giving the advice.

Current consumer AI apps such as Glamify and roboMUA work out a person's skin shade from a selfie or live camera. They then recommend shade-matched foundation, lip and eye products and give step-by-step routines and tutorials. This covers the color- and type-advice part of the task.

Brand and enterprise tools, including Maybelline's Virtual Beauty Studio and Perfect Corp's YouCam tutorial and shade-finder SDKs, offer virtual try-on and guided makeup tutorials from a camera feed. Accuracy depends on lighting and photo conditions, and a person still has to demonstrate on the client's face and correct their technique in person.

Esthetician licensing, for example in California, covers applying makeup for pay. Advising clients and teaching techniques is not shown to need a licensed person's signature, and many states do not license makeup artistry at all.

USPS buys driverless tow tractors and pallet trucks to move mail containers around processing plants. This is robotic hardware, not a software AI agent. A software agent could at most send moves through a fleet-management system it would not normally have access to.
Moving mail containers means physically driving, hitching and staging carts, OTR containers and powered industrial trucks on the workroom floor.
Similar autonomous tugs in parcel hubs, such as UPS Tacoma, depend on physical robots that navigate with lasers. A software-only agent has no body and cannot do this.

Barn feeding and cleaning are automated by dedicated robots and mechanical systems (feeding robots, manure scrapers), not by software-only AI agents. Without those robots, the work needs someone physically present to handle feed, water and disinfection.
Robots for cleaning pig barns and cattle feeders are still in research or development, so cleaning and disinfecting pens and cages remains largely manual work.

Automated feeding and watering systems are physical installations that run on their own control logic. A software agent could at most adjust schedules on a connected controller, which is a small part of the task.

EID readers and scale indicators store each weight against the animal's tag and sync it to software automatically. The software then calculates average daily gain and growth trends without anyone typing the numbers in.

Farmbrite says (vendor claim) its software links EID scans to automated weighing scales and feed stations, and tracks daily weight gain, feed consumption and feed efficiency per animal. Someone still has to handle the animals physically and keep the hardware running.

The iLivestock app logs weights and medicines, monitors growth, and exports weighing sessions as CSV files. These are digital records that an agent could consolidate and analyse, but the measurements themselves are taken on the farm.

Computer-assisted semen analysis (CASA) systems already measure sperm motility, kinematics and concentration automatically. Someone still has to collect the sample, load the slide and work the microscope and analyzer.

Concentration and motility (total and progressive) are the values used to work out how many doses an ejaculate can yield. That calculation is the part of the job an agent could do in software, along with recording the results.

CASA accuracy depends on methodological factors and microscopy limits, and the slide prep and extender mixing are hands-on work in the lab. Because of this, an AI agent with no body cannot do the core steps of the task.
AI tools for warehouses are sold as 'digital co-pilots' for supervisors. They flag exceptions and help troubleshoot, but they support human expertise rather than replace it.

AutoScheduler.AI's Warehouse Decision Agent answers voice questions from the floor about late shipments and labor decisions and gives recommendations, so it helps with analysis inside problem-solving that humans still lead.

O*NET lists collaboration with workers and managers alongside floor-based duties such as monitoring safety and reviewing work as it happens. These are in-person roles under job titles like Floor Supervisor and Warehouse Supervisor.

Vendor guides describe AI agents that check every timesheet entry against dispatch records and job codes, flag overtime anomalies, cross-check GPS data, and send only the exceptions to a person for a decision. That covers the main record-keeping and verification steps, but a human still reviews the flagged exceptions and approves the result.

Agentic reconciliation tools compare time logs with badge or access data, schedules, project plans and budgets, and send suspect entries to managers. This automates checking time and expense records against each other.

For driver hours-of-service records (ELD), the driver certifies each 24-hour record and the driver and carrier share responsibility for accuracy. I found no rule requiring a supervisor to personally sign these records, so the legal barrier to delegation is low. Some records still depend on human attestation, and physically checking materials or observing crews on site stays with people.

Econolite's Centracs MMS is a maintenance module that runs alone or with the Centracs ATMS. It supports user-defined preventive maintenance plans and schedules, mobile reporting of work activities, and a map of active work orders, so writing the work order is already a software task.

Trimble AgileAssets Signal/ITS has configurable workflows for work requests and creates work orders. It turns annual plans and problem reports into actual work orders, which shows the main sub-steps can be automated without anyone on site.

OxMaint says its product connects to traffic management systems and controller cabinet data feeds and opens priority work orders when a controller faults. This is an unverified vendor claim. It still means the remaining human work is mostly judging site conditions and approving changes to signal timing or devices, not writing the order.
Perfect Corp's YouCam AI/AR nail tools let users and retailers virtually try on nail colors, styles, shapes and press-ons in real time, which covers product and color advice in software.

State manicurist licenses (e.g. Texas TDLR) cover hands-on nail services such as trimming, polishing and attaching false nails. They do not require a licensed human to give general nail care or product advice.

Boards such as California's keep conditions like calluses outside the manicurist's scope. Advice therefore depends on looking at the client's hands or feet, which usually happens in person during the service.

An OSHA interpretation letter describes the work: a crane lifts monuments of about 100 to 1,700 lb from the delivery truck bed onto a pre-installed foundation or a heavy-duty cart. It is hands-on rigging and equipment operation at the grave site, which a software-only agent cannot do.

OSHA's crane rules (29 CFR 1926.1427) require operators of larger cranes to be certified through written and practical tests, and some states add stricter licensing. A qualified human has to run the hoist or crane.

Truck crane operation requires a practical test showing safe hands-on operation. Small cranes rated at about 2,000 lb or less are exempt from certification, but someone still has to operate them physically.

Vendors such as Board, Prophix and Lucanet released FP&A, controller and treasury AI agents in 2026. These agents keep rolling forecasts and scenario plans up to date and build models from prompts. Human-in-the-loop controls on significant decisions are still the norm.

Directors' and officers' duty of care, which includes acting on an informed basis, means AI is unlikely to replace human judgment on financial decisions. Courts may expect fiduciaries to test AI outputs against their own judgment.
Practitioner guidance says AI can produce forecasts, spot trends and suggest actions, but should not have the final say on financial recommendations to leadership.

Aircraft whole-air samplers such as NOAA's PFP and the Medusa sampler on ATom fill flasks automatically on a preprogrammed schedule, so software can trigger and log samples. Installing the hardware, handling the flasks and running the flight operations still has to be done in person.

NCAR's Advanced Whole Air Sampler (AWAS) is a certified instrument installed on the HIAPER aircraft. It collects samples into stainless steel canisters that are taken off the plane and analyzed later, which requires physical installation, retrieval and transport.

In UC Irvine's proposed SEAC4RS whole-air sampling on the NASA DC-8, scientists on board would collect up to 168 canister samples per flight. Researchers on the aircraft do the sampling, while an AI agent's help would be limited to planning, the sampling schedule and data logging.

2026 research systems use LLMs to compare source and translation, mark span-level MQM errors and post-edit them. Their error annotations agree strongly with human MQM judgments, so the agent can run the check of the original against the translation end to end.

A large production study (EAMT 2026) of AI post-editing across 10 languages still relied on 60 professional translators to judge quality. Human review is still used to confirm meaning and tone before the work is used.
ISO 17100 requires a second person to revise translations. This is a voluntary quality standard, not a legal licence, but it keeps a human reviser in the workflow under common industry practice.

Job descriptions for correctional sergeants say they directly supervise officers, do rounds, check logbooks, run head counts and shakedowns, and respond to emergencies, including using force and chemical agents. All of this happens on site in the facility.

A Michigan sergeant position description puts about 40% of the job into directing custody and housing officers, including checking work-area rounds and logbooks. Virginia's class description defines the sergeant as the first-line supervisor of officers who also reviews logs and reports and evaluates staff.

Industry and county reports from 2026 describe AI in jails as a support tool for scheduling, movement tracking, documentation and monitoring alerts, freeing staff for direct supervision rather than replacing it.
Correctional sergeants run roll call at the start of each shift. They check who is present, assign officers to posts, and inspect their appearance, equipment and any contraband in person.
Philadelphia's job spec says the sergeant inspects guards for appearance, equipment and contraband, which has to be done physically.

Corrections scheduling software such as UKG TeleStaff already handles post rosters, staffing levels and attendance tracking. That covers the clerical parts of roll call, but the in-person muster, inspection and briefing still need a human.

School nutrition inventory tools such as PrimeroEdge with IntelliScan, Nutrikids and Meals Plus already track product usage, purchases, variance and costs. Staff still scan receipts and count stock physically using UPC codes.

Invoice-scanning tools such as ShelfCount capture receipt data automatically and hold price changes for approval before records are updated. This automates the expenditure side of record-keeping, but a human still checks it.

Institutional foodservice suites such as CBORD handle cafeteria inventory, purchasing and cost records. Once usage and invoice data are entered, an agent with system access could compile and maintain them.

Vendor material describes AI agents in maintenance software that rank the work backlog, schedule work, create purchase requisitions and choose a vendor by lead time and cost. The requisition still goes to a human for approval. These are marketing claims and have not been checked independently.

Vendor management software for property maintenance teams handles contractor scheduling and work-order dispatch digitally. This covers the 'arrange' part of the task. This is a vendor product page, not an independent evaluation.

Not shown by either source above (inference): the recommendation part depends on someone physically inspecting worn furnishings, damage and paint condition on site, plus local judgment on budget. Spending approval normally stays with a human manager. No licence or legal requirement applies to the supervisor's recommendation.
Housekeeping apps send each room status change to the property management system (PMS) in real time, so the front desk can see which rooms are ready without phoning a supervisor.
Housekeeping software can mark a room as ready automatically once it passes inspection, so no one has to re-enter the status in a second system. That covers most of the communication step.

Maestro PMS automatically texts guests when their room is ready, as soon as the front office receives the new status from housekeeping. A person still has to inspect the room and enter that status, and that step needs someone on site.

In airline and union checklists, preparing for landing means physical walkthroughs. Flight attendants check that passengers are seated with belts fastened and that seatbacks and tray tables are up. They also latch bins and closets, check lavatories, and stow galley and service items. An agent with no body cannot do any of this.

Part 121 rules give these duties to certificated flight attendants. They must secure the cabin and galley for landing, then stay belted in their assigned jumpseats from landing until the aircraft parks at the gate. A human crewmember is legally accountable for this.

The only part that is automated so far is announcements. A patent describes pre-recorded announcements triggered by flight phase, and Pegasus uses AI-synthesised voices for some languages. Crew still make the main announcements and do all physical cabin checks.

Pre-recorded announcements are stored on the Flight Attendant Panel (FAP), and newer units can be loaded from USB sticks. Crew can power down a misbehaving IFE at the flight attendant panel or cabin management terminal, which means using onboard hardware in person.
When IFE malfunctions, crew reset the system at the individual seat or, on older aircraft, for whole blocks of seats. PA announcements pause or override IFE.

The system already automates some of this: it can store and replay standard safety, boarding and arrival messages in several languages at the touch of a button. Regulations require a working interphone/PA system on commercial transport aircraft.

SITA's WorldTracer Bag Mate is a managed service that runs the mishandled-baggage process from the passenger's report to the bag's return or compensation. It uses a hybrid of AI agents and SITA-trained human agents, so humans are still part of the process (vendor claim).
With WorldTracer Baggage Self-Service, passengers report and track delayed bags digitally. In Lufthansa Group trials, two-thirds of passengers chose it over the baggage counter.
Aeromexico's Aerobot chatbot pulls a missing bag's status from WorldTracer through its API without a human agent, so automated status lookup has been in use since 2019.

To run excavators and bulldozers on their own, Built Robotics fits each machine with an aftermarket hardware kit (Exosystem) that includes an enclosure, radar, 360° cameras and GPS. This is robotic hardware on the machine, which a software-only AI agent does not have.

Bedrock Robotics' autonomous excavation also relies on retrofitted machines. It streams video and machine data to a cloud platform where human supervisors step in when needed, so even purpose-built autonomy keeps people in the loop.
Built Robotics' autonomy is used mainly in narrow niches such as solar piling and trenching. Ordinary bulldozers, graders and backhoes still need an operator in the cab working the levers and pedals.
Accenture/Avanade/Microsoft's 'agentic factory' agents give operators and supervisors guided troubleshooting, suggest likely causes and draft maintenance tickets, but people keep the final decisions.

Manufacturing quality-control agents pull together sensor, inspection and maintenance data and send summaries with evidence to engineers and operators, but much operator knowledge sits in silos that the agent cannot reach.
CausalTrace is an academic agent that does root-cause analysis with real-time operator interaction on an assembly testbed. It supports human problem-solving rather than replacing the operator.

Existing CAD add-ons such as BlankWorks, NESTINGWorks and Solid Edge's sheet-metal and nesting tools already turn 3D designs into flat patterns and nested layouts, accounting for stretch, bend radii and thickness. So the trigonometry and pattern-development steps can be done in software an agent can operate.

O*NET shows the role is tied to physical workpieces: workers mark lines and holes with scribes, soapstones and punches, check templates with measuring instruments, and fit parts before welding. Planning the layout depends on physical stock and templates that an agent cannot handle or check.

Automatic nesting tools for sheet metal, such as NestIt released for IronCAD in 2026, organize flat patterns by material and quantity. This supports delegating the digital layout-planning steps, while shop-floor judgment about heat distortion and the material still needs a human to review it.

Fuel-logging software such as Fluidyne FuelLog and AW Company's fuel monitor reads boiler fuel flow meters and produces consumption reports on its own. Spirax Sarco's B850 boilerhouse monitor tracks fuel use from historical trend data. So on metered plants an agent could pull, check and log the data without a person doing each step.

Job descriptions say boiler operators read meters and gauges and log the fuel consumed at set intervals. Where meters aren't connected, that means walking the plant, dipping tanks and weighing coal, which needs someone physically there.

Most US states require a licence to operate a boiler, but no source found requires a licensed person to sign the fuel-use records themselves. Licensing covers operating the boiler, not keeping the log.

Yard management systems already record railcar arrival and departure times, dwell and track status automatically from AEI tag reads, wheel sensors and cameras. Crew apps such as Wabtec mCrew let crews report arrivals, departures, pickups and set-outs digitally.

Electronic hours-of-service records are allowed under 49 CFR Part 228, but the employee or reporting crew member must certify them, and each record is stamped with the certifier's name and the certification time. A human still has to sign off on time on duty.

FRA requires electronic hours-of-service recordkeeping systems to meet set technical rules and to give inspectors access. The data sits in railroad-controlled systems that an outside agent would not normally reach.

Agents can already be connected to Canvas through its API and MCP integrations. Through those they can read gradebook data and grading activity, so they can pull together grade summaries and prepare paperwork before a meeting.
In current AI-assisted grading setups, a human reviews grades before they are posted to the LMS. Grade decisions still get a person's approval.
University policy makes the instructor of record responsible for submitting final grades, so a human must sign off on grade paperwork.

Bedside tablet and app ordering systems in hospitals, such as CBORD Patient App and menuPick, let patients pick meals and set diet and allergy preferences digitally. The order is then delivered to the bedside, but staff still have to carry it out in person.
At UCSF Mission Bay, every bed has a bedside tablet for meal ordering, but only about half of patients use it. The rest still order by phone, so the order capture part is only partly automated.

Some vendor systems have staff take orders at the bedside on touchscreens and support either traditional or room service delivery. Settling patients in to eat, such as positioning them, the tray and the table, still requires a physical presence.

Mashgin's countertop checkout uses several cameras and computer-vision AI to identify packaged items and plated food in cafeterias without a cashier. This is dedicated kiosk hardware, not a software-only agent.

Autocanteen's vendor page claims its AI checkout identifies meal plates in about 10 seconds per transaction, with one assistant overseeing several checkout points. Supervision and cash handling still fall to a person, and these figures are marketing claims that have not been independently verified.

An Intel brief describes camera-based self-checkout systems that take over item recognition and billing in food service. Taking cash, making change and handling the trays are still physical work that a bodiless software agent cannot do.
Bars slice citrus garnish by hand or with manual pull-handle and lever wedgers (Nemco Easy Wedger, Prince Castle CW-6). This is physical knife or tool work that a software-only agent cannot do.
Automated fruit wedge-cutting machines appear in patents, but these are hardware, not AI agents. The task is about manipulating fruit, and no law or licence requires a specific person to do it.
Commercial lemon slicers range from handheld cutters to countertop units. All of them need a person to load and operate them.

Vendor pages say AI scheduling agents for landscaping plan crew routes by zip code and crew skill, send reminders and handle weather-driven reschedules across the customer base. This is marketing material, not an independent benchmark.

FieldProxy says its tool plans crew routes using traffic, how long each property takes, crew skills, equipment needs and time-of-day limits, and that on rain days it finds the affected jobs and suggests new times. These are vendor claims.

A competitor comparison says some field-service tools such as ServiceM8 still make dispatchers move weather-affected jobs by hand. That suggests a supervisor still checks and adjusts the schedule using what they know about the sites and crews. This is one vendor writing about a rival.

AI add-ons for maintenance work-order systems read requests from email, text, calls, Slack and forms, then create or route work orders as a 24/7 digital coordinator. This covers the routine information-passing between units.

Facilities AI assistants can be trained on a team's own procedures to sort and route requests across departments and show request trends to facilities leaders. Agreeing on priorities and committing crews still falls to the human supervisor.

Agentic AI for facilities is described as ranking urgency, scheduling against staff availability and resource limits, and grouping related tasks. These are sub-steps of coordinating work between units, but the negotiation between supervisors is still done by people, often face to face.

FieldProxy's landscaping blueprint, a vendor workflow, describes AI scoring of photos from completed jobs. It flags defects such as missed mowing strips or uneven edges, sends low-scoring jobs to a supervisor's mobile dashboard, and turns rejected items into follow-up tasks for the crew. This automates issuing corrective work orders, but a person still has to take the photos on site.

OrangeQC's groundskeeper inspection software captures inspection checklists with photos and GPS tags, plus corrective-action tickets that can be assigned and tracked. The ordering and tracking are digital, but the inspection depends on someone being physically at the site.

None of the sources found shows a law or licence requiring a human to order corrective landscape work or recommend procedural changes. The physical fix is done by crews, and the supervisor has to judge problems at the site and convince crews to change how they work.

Landscaping route-optimization software takes a list of service addresses and produces efficient crew routes automatically. Vendors claim it cuts in-field travel time by up to 25-30%, but these figures are not independently verified.

Landscaping fleet software combines GPS data with maintenance scheduling and cost tracking, which supports data-driven decisions about equipment and vehicles. An agent with access to these systems could analyze the data and draft recommendations.

GPS and time-tracking apps record crew arrival and departure times automatically. This gives productivity data an agent could analyze, but seeing on-site working conditions and how equipment performs still needs a person in the field.

Irrigation design software, including CAD plugins and web planners, already automates zone layout, sprinkler placement, pipe sizing and pressure-loss calculations. Vendors still advise checking the results with engineering judgment.
In Texas, San Antonio's water utility requires a licensed person to be present and supervise each new irrigation installation, and a city permit must be issued for the work.
Connecticut says it is illegal to install an irrigation system without a license. Controller low-voltage wiring must be done by a licensed contractor, and local permits are required.

Free tools like TeeJet SpraySelect already suggest nozzle tips, target pressure and flow rate from speed, spacing, application rate and droplet size. This covers the selection step, which an AI agent can also do. The hoses and nozzles still have to be fitted by hand.
A smartphone calibration write-up shows the app gives a per-nozzle flow target. The operator then checks output with a timed catch test on the sprayer itself, which is physical work.

Federal rules say non-certified people may use restricted-use pesticides only under a certified applicator's direct supervision. For some products this means the supervisor must be physically present. The rules govern handling, not specifically connecting equipment, so the main barrier to this task is physical rather than legal.

O*NET lists Construction Laborers (47-2061.00) as workers who do physical labor at construction sites. Their tasks include installing sewer, water or storm drain pipes with pipe-laying machinery or laser guidance equipment. That work needs a person on site, and a software-only agent cannot do it.
DOL seasonal job postings describe laborers carrying, positioning, holding and supporting pipe materials, backfilling trenches, and helping join components. All of this is hands-on manual handling.

The O*NET summary describes the occupation as physical labor that helps other craft workers on site. Software can only play a small side role, such as looking up specs or alignment tolerances, and a person still has to do the positioning, joining and sealing.

Operator competency standards for this work are all hands-on site work: checking floor machines, removing debris and adhesives, choosing machine speed, rotation and diamond tools, and running overlapping, staggered passes while watching motor load. A software-only agent with no robotics cannot do any of these steps.
Manual grinders are still common, and the quality of the finish depends heavily on the operator's skill. Riding multi-head machines also need an operator on site.

OSHA's silica standard (29 CFR 1926.1153, Table 1) treats concrete grinding as an on-site, high-exposure task that needs dust controls and sometimes respirators. It regulates worker safety but does not require a licensed human to perform or sign off the work.

Glazier software's AI-assisted takeoff reads uploaded floor plans, finds the glazing scope, applies default glass and edgework templates, and exports to estimates or purchase orders. The user still makes selections and reviews the result before exporting.

Ruh AI says (vendor marketing, not verified) its glazing takeoff measures curtain wall by system from elevations, measures storefront in linear feet, counts openings and separates glass area using the elevations and schedules.

General AI takeoff tools such as Bobyard and Attentive automatically extract quantities from construction drawings. The search found no tool that produces a full lite-by-lite glass makeup straight from drawings, and no tool that plans staging or scaffolding from site conditions. Those steps still rely on human judgment and field checks.

Battery terminal cleaning is hands-on physical work: disconnecting terminals, scrubbing with a wire brush and baking-soda paste, rinsing, drying and reconnecting, while wearing gloves and eye protection.
Corrosive battery acid makes PPE and physical handling necessary. Software can do no more than give guidance, such as safety steps or which cleaner to use for heavy buildup.
Substations are restricted to qualified persons, so supervising splicing on site needs a qualified human who is physically there.

Splicing and termination supervision is a field role held by a sub-foreman who splices and terminates XLPE, PILC and PR cables. An agent could only help with scheduling, color-code schedules and records.
Checking that the color-code sequence was followed is done by visual inspection of the physical termination. Wiring color schedules follow ICEA E-1 and E-2, which software can document.
O*NET lists polishing instruments with rags and polishing compounds, buffing wheels or burnishing tools as a hands-on task for musical instrument repairers.

Professional polishing is physical work: a buffing wheel is used first with Tripoli compound to cut out scratches, then with red rouge to bring up the color. A software-only agent with no robotics cannot do this.
Before re-buffing, the instrument usually has to be taken apart and the old lacquer stripped with solvents, which are more hands-on steps. No licence or sign-off rule applies to this task.

Shot peen operators read blueprints and work orders, then lay out and mark peen areas by measuring and marking or by fitting templates and peeling maskant. They also fill hoppers with the specified shot size and type. All of this is hands-on work.
Specifications require no-peen areas to be physically masked with maskant, tape or rubber/metal masks. An AI agent could only help by reading drawings and specs or suggesting a layout.
O*NET lists this task for CNC Tool Operators (51-9161.00).
Melt-shop molten-metal sampling is automated with dedicated robots, such as the SMS X-Pact Sampler built on ABB or COMAU arms. That is physical robotics. A software-only AI agent cannot do it.

Polytec's PolySAMPLE robot takes molten-metal samples and temperature readings with little human involvement. Its stated purpose is keeping workers out of the hazardous area next to the melt, which shows the task needs a physical presence there.

Robots handling sublance sampling probes at voestalpine Linz replaced manual work at the furnace. The automation is in the hardware. A software agent could at most send the sampling signal or log the request, which is a small part of the task.

Furnace loading is automated only with dedicated industrial robots, such as 6-axis or FANUC arms with grippers and vision that place parts in baskets, fixtures or on furnace belts. A software-only AI agent has no such physical capability.
Robotic furnace loaders for conveyor and sinter furnaces are custom hardware cells, for example the Adaptec Model 100A with a magnetic gripper. This confirms the task means physically handling parts.

Heat treat operations have traditionally relied on manual loading and batch transfer, and placing parts correctly in baskets affects how evenly they heat and how much they distort. This is physical handling work that is done in person.

Colour-matching software such as X-Rite Color iMatch suggests dye formulas and searches past recipes. It still needs spectrophotometer measurements and a physical lab dip made and checked by the dyer, so a human does the physical matching and the AI only assists.

Datacolor Match Textile handles dye compatibility and colour shifts after dyeing when building a formula. It helps with knowing dye properties, but it relies on measurement hardware that small dry cleaners usually don't have.

Commercial colour matching starts by measuring a physical sample with a spectrophotometer, followed by dyeing fabric lab dips by hand. Both steps need someone physically present to handle the garment, dyes and bleaching agents.

Cabinet design packages such as Cabinet Vision, KCD, SketchList 3D and Mozaik build cut lists and CNC-ready output from a 3D design. KCD checks that measurements and machining instructions are consistent. These tools cover much of the work of setting specifications and planning operations, but a human still enters the design.

A 2026 roundup lists AI-assisted cabinet design tools. One of them, WoodWright, claims to cover design, cut lists and CNC output, but its listing is a third-party review. I found no confirmed product that turns scanned 2D drawings straight into a buildable model, so a human still has to review and correct the output.

Cabinetmaker trade certification is voluntary in every Canadian province and territory. Australian licensing applies to on-site installation, not to reading drawings or planning work, so no licence requires a human to sign this task.

Setting knives means unplugging the machine, placing a jig on the cutterhead, loosening the set screws, raising or lowering each knife to the right height and tightening it again. Every step is done by hand at the machine.

Automatic tool changers on CNC routers swap bits on their own, but people still load and preset the tool holders by hand. That is automation built into the machine, not a software agent doing the job.
Workers must use safe practices such as isolation and lock-outs while setting up the machine. This is a workplace safety rule, not a licence or sign-off requirement.

Manufacturing job postings describe this work as loading, unloading, stacking and staging materials with forklifts and pallet jacks, moving raw materials to production lines, and lifting up to 50 lb. All of it is physical handling that an agent without a body cannot do.
OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(l) says that only trained and authorized operators may run powered industrial trucks. Employers must certify each operator's training and evaluation.
Some forklift roles include inventory tracking and recording shipping and receiving. That paperwork is the only digital part of the job an agent could do, and it is a small share of the work time.

Cutting CAD/CAM software such as ESAB Columbus Job Wizard can generate NC programs from customer orders automatically, nest parts on plates and assign a machine. An agent could do the program-preparation part of 'typing instructions'.

SigmaNEST automates programming for profile cutting machines (laser, plasma, waterjet, router, punch) and batch-processes BOMs and work orders. The software side can be automated, but the operator still loads, starts and sets up the machine.

Hypertherm ProNest Production Manager connects to EDGE Connect CNCs for automatic data capture and remote access. Only some networked machines can be reached this way; manually setting guides, clamps and knives at the machine needs a person there.
